When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents

Runxuan Tang Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Email: TANG0609@e.ntu.edu.sg    Haoyu Gao Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: gao.howard517@gmail.com    Yuyan Ding Affiliation: University of Washington Email: yuyand2@uw.edu    Junyi Yao Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis Email: j.yao@wustl.edu    Zihao Zheng Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis Email: z.zihaogary@wustl.edu    Zecheng Sheng Affiliation: The University of Sydney Email: zshe0457@uni.sydney.edu.au    Liwei Hou Email: liweihou@u.nus.edu*Equal contribution.†Corresponding author. Affiliation: National University of Singapore
Abstract

LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass1 on τ\tau-Retail/τ\tau-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to operate in long-horizon, interactive environments where they must reason, call tools, update internal context, and recover from mistakes (Yao et al., 2023). This capability supports web navigation, app-level tool use, and user-facing assistance (Zhou et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024); embodied interaction additionally requires grounding language in visual and gestural context (Li et al., 2023). Continual deployment requires agents to solve current tasks and safely learn reusable behavioral knowledge from experience.

Recent work has made substantial progress toward self-improving agents through self-feedback and reflection (Madaan et al., 2023), verbal reinforcement from past failures (Shinn et al., 2023), reusable skill memory (Wang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026b), agentic long-term memory organization (Xu et al., 2025), and evolving symbolic contexts or playbooks (Zhou et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026f). These methods show that storing lessons, memories, playbooks, or revised contexts can improve future performance without necessarily updating model weights. An episode-derived update may improve tasks that resemble the triggering episode while overgeneralizing to superficially similar but semantically different situations, conflicting with previously successful behaviors, or accumulating as stale persistent memory. Even in verifier-rich environments, where task success can often be checked after execution, existing self-evolution mechanisms lack a principled criterion for assessing an update’s transferability, retention value, and commitment risk. The central question is how to govern the transition from temporary experience to persistent agent state under transfer, safety, and regression constraints.

We study when an experience-derived behavioral update should enter an LLM agent’s long-term memory. Our approach treats persistent updates as testable hypotheses. As shown in Fig. 1, our approach temporarily applies each candidate update, evaluates its transfer beyond the source episode, robustness to targeted counterexamples, and preservation of archived successful behavior, and then commits, refines, or rejects it.

We make the following contributions: (i) We identify a core failure mode of self-evolving agents: target improvement alone is an unreliable signal for persistent memory writing, because many apparently useful updates encode unsafe shortcuts or overly broad applicability conditions. (ii) We introduce Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that treats candidate updates as testable hypotheses and performs structured commit–refine–reject triage before long-term retention. (iii) Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory settings, FGSE improves task performance while reducing falsification failures, regression damage, harmful committed updates, and post-commit violations compared with reflection-, memory-, and context-evolution baselines.

2 Related Work

Interactive language agents and verifier-rich environments. LLM agents combine reasoning with external actions, from ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) to tool use (Qin et al., 2024; Chen and Liu, 2026; Xiao et al., 2026b), while LLM-derived traffic context also augments motion prediction (Zheng et al., 2024). This progress has enabled realistic web, app, and tool-use benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024), where success can often be checked by executable validators, database states, user goals, or safety constraints. Healthcare-agent evaluation protocols additionally assess episode-level state continuity, evidence traceability, and escalation decisions (Yao et al., 2026). Complementary work verifies and repairs synthetic web environments before agent training (Zhang et al., 2026a). A YANG-grounded LLM agent supports multi-vendor OpenROADM management through schema retrieval and validation of generated configurations (Xiao et al., 2026c). Complementary network-diagnosis work uses multi-head graph attention to jointly address alarm correlation and root alarm detection in optical transport networks (Xiao et al., 2025). Medical-agent security combines risk perception, evidence constraints, and knowledge-consistency verification (Hu, 2026). Broader security research studies quantitative vulnerability assessment (Shao, 2026b), SHAP-based explanations for network anomaly detection (Shao, 2026a), APT attribution over heterogeneous threat knowledge graphs (Wang et al., 2026), and provenance-graph anomaly detection (Ma et al., 2026). FGSE builds on verifier-rich settings and applies verification to candidate behavioral updates before persistent commitment, testing transfer, falsification, and regression safety.

Memory and context-based self-improvement. Another line improves agents without updating model weights. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) revise future behavior through self-feedback or verbal reinforcement, while Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) stores reusable executable skills. Persistent-memory systems such as Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), and A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025) organize memories for retrieval, reflection, and personalization, with LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) evaluating long-horizon memory utility. Recent context-evolution methods, including Symbolic Learning (Zhou et al., 2025), Lighthouse (Yang et al., 2025), and ACE (Zhang et al., 2026f), further revise prompts, playbooks, critiques, or contexts from execution feedback. These methods show that textual updates can improve agents, but they may overgeneralize local lessons, accumulate stale or conflicting memories, or degrade useful context during iterative rewriting, echoing concerns about unreliable self-correction (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026b) and unsafe misevolution (Shao et al., 2026). Adjacent retrieval studies distinguish semantic relevance from factual consistency in RAG (Ye et al., 2026) and show benefits of exemplar diversity under matched context budgets for multi-turn intent understanding (Lin et al., 2026). FGSE treats each lesson as a structured, verifier-grounded hypothesis and commits it only after falsification and regression testing.

Capability-level contribution evidence. Xu et al. (2026c) propose an observable evidence standard for added planning capabilities, separating presence, opportunity to act, executed-plan change, and incremental operational consequence under controlled replay, with explicit treatment of equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Their analysis requires capability-specific contribution evidence for acceptance, beyond aggregate policy gains or proxy diagnostics. For memory updates, contribution likewise depends on verified behavioral effects beyond storage or retrieval. FGSE evaluates each update against the current agent in a temporary state and requires target-transfer gain, falsification resistance, and regression preservation before commitment (Eq. (8)); subsequent activation requires a matching precondition and a violation record below threshold (Section 4.3). These conditions link contribution evidence to verification and bounded activation of memory updates.

Automated agent optimization and self-evolution. Beyond memory writing, recent work optimizes agent systems by searching over prompts, graph structures, workflows, or multi-agent state machines (Yang et al., 2024; Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b), and improves reasoning policies through test-time reinforcement learning, self-generated curricula, or tool-integrated co-evolution (Zuo et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2025). In Text-to-SQL, an autonomy-based taxonomy highlights execution-guided self-correction and modular agent collaboration (Su et al., 2027). Continual adaptation also studies how to preserve knowledge under bounded resources: CoMem (Zhou et al., 2026) uses concept-graph memory and feature-space rehearsal for vision–language adaptation; InduceKV (Chen et al., 2026) externalizes multimodal adaptation into budgeted key–value memories; and Meta-UCF (Xiao et al., 2026d) generates task-conditioned LoRA updates with a shared hypernetwork. Compo-ReAlign (Xiao et al., 2026a) preserves compositional structure through reversible alignment and sensitivity-constrained updates, while Affordance-First Decomposition (Xu et al., 2026b) separates a stable affordance substrate from query-routed, conflict-aware adaptation in video–language learning. These lines address adaptation capacity, retention, and resource efficiency, alongside cross-domain studies of recoverable model pruning (Lu et al., 2026), multi-scale and attention-based visual processing (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026d), activation design and LLM-guided fusion for forecasting (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c), and operational decision making through semantic evidence for inspection allocation (He et al., 2026), causal intervention ranking (Huang et al., 2026b), and accuracy–stability trade-offs in forecasting (Li et al., 2026a). FGSE addresses a complementary update-level problem: it falsifies each episode-derived update before persistent commitment, preserving self-evolution plasticity while controlling unsafe transfer and regression.

3 Preliminary Study

A common self-improvement strategy is to summarize completed episodes into reflective text or experiential insights and store them in memory for future decision making (Shinn et al., 2023). While such updates can help on similar tasks, they may overgeneralize, disrupt previously solved behaviors, or encode brittle shortcuts. We characterize these failure modes in a diagnostic study.

Diagnostic setup. For each completed episode, the base agent generates a free-form update uu, such as a rule, reminder, or behavioral correction, which we inject into the memory prompt and compare against the original agent. For analysis, we evaluate uu on four case groups: source replay, near transfer, boundary contrast, and archived success, corresponding to the original episode neighborhood, intended-pattern transfer, superficially similar non-trigger cases, and previously solved tasks. For each group 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we measure the average verifier-score change induced by uu:

Δ𝒞​(u)=1|𝒞|​∑x∈𝒞[J⁡(Θ⊕u,x)−J⁡(Θ,x)],\Delta_{\mathcal{C}}(u)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\left[J(\Theta\oplus u,x)-J(\Theta,x)\right], (1)

where Θ\Theta is the original agent state and Θ⊕u\Theta\oplus u denotes the same agent with the free-form lesson uu appended to memory. We report near-transfer gain Δnear​(u)\Delta_{\mathrm{near}}(u), boundary harm [−Δboundary​(u)]+[-\Delta_{\mathrm{boundary}}(u)]_{+}, and archive harm [−Δarchive​(u)]+[-\Delta_{\mathrm{archive}}(u)]_{+}. We also annotate each lesson with a coarse scope-specificity score in [0,1][0,1], where lower values indicate broader and less conditional updates.

Findings. Figure 2 shows that naive memory writing is useful but unreliable. Free-form lessons often improve near-transfer cases but can cause boundary harm, indicating that locally valid behaviors may be applied in inappropriate contexts. This failure is closely tied to scope: broad, underspecified lessons produce larger boundary and archive degradation than more specific ones, and sequentially writing them into memory accumulates errors despite short-term source gains. Post-hoc localization further shows that some harmful updates contain valid rules with overly broad applicability; narrowing their scope can retain transfer benefits while reducing harm. These findings motivate FGSE, which treats episode-derived lessons as structured, falsifiable hypotheses, tests them temporarily on target, boundary, and archived cases, and commits or refines them only when supported by evidence.

4 Method

4.1 Overview

We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework for reliable long-term improvement of language agents. Given an episode, FGSE converts the observed success or failure into a structured behavioral hypothesis that specifies its precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. The hypothesis is applied only temporarily and evaluated on target-transfer probes and falsification probes. It is committed to persistent agent state only when it improves target cases, survives targeted falsification, and preserves previously solved behavior. Hypotheses with localized failures are refined once through precondition narrowing and reevaluated; hypotheses that still fail are rejected. Figure 3 summarizes the pipeline, with probe construction and refinement details provided in Appendix A.2 and Appendix A.3.

4.2 Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution

Verifier-grounded agent state.

At episode tt, the agent receives a task xtx_{t} and acts under persistent state

Θt=(ℳt,πt),Jv(Θ,x)=𝔼τ∼pΘ(⋅∣x)[v(x,τ)].\Theta_{t}=(\mathcal{M}_{t},\pi_{t}),\qquad J_{v}(\Theta,x)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\Theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[v(x,\tau)\right]. (2)

Here, ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} is the retrievable memory of committed evolution units, πt\pi_{t} is the current agent policy, pΘ​(τ∣x)p_{\Theta}(\tau\mid x) is the trajectory distribution induced by state Θ\Theta on task xx, and v⁡(x,τ)∈[0,1]v(x,\tau)\in[0,1] is a verifier-grounded score. The expectation accounts for stochastic decoding, tool uncertainty, and multi-step interaction. A completed episode yields a trajectory τt\tau_{t} and verifier result rt=vt​(xt,τt)r_{t}=v_{t}(x_{t},\tau_{t}), from which FGSE forms an evidence packet Et=(xt,τt,rt,𝒜t)E_{t}=(x_{t},\tau_{t},r_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}) using the audit archive 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}.

Structured evolution hypothesis.

Each candidate update is represented as

h=(ch,bh,eh,vh).h=(c_{h},b_{h},e_{h},v_{h}). (3)

The precondition ch:𝒵→[0,1]c_{h}:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow[0,1] assigns an applicability score to an interaction state z=(x,τ<ℓ)z=(x,\tau_{<\ell}). The behavior transformation bhb_{h} maps the current policy to a modified policy bh​[πΘ]b_{h}[\pi_{\Theta}]. The expected-effect checker ehe_{h} specifies the verifier-observable outcome that should hold after applying the update. The verifier vhv_{h} provides the task-level score used to evaluate improvement, failure, and regression. The proposer HϕH_{\phi} maps the evidence packet to a schema-constrained hypothesis, ht=Hϕ​(Et)h_{t}=H_{\phi}(E_{t}). The proposer generates candidates; the commitment gate determines their retention.

The hypothesis is activated only when its precondition is satisfied:

gh(z)=𝕀[ch(z)≥γh],πΘt⊕h(a∣z)=(1−λhgh(z))πΘt(a∣z)+λhgh(z)bh[πΘt](a∣z).g_{h}(z)=\mathbb{I}[c_{h}(z)\geq\gamma_{h}],\qquad\pi_{\Theta_{t}\oplus h}(a\mid z)=(1-\lambda_{h}g_{h}(z))\pi_{\Theta_{t}}(a\mid z)+\lambda_{h}g_{h}(z)b_{h}[\pi_{\Theta_{t}}](a\mid z). (4)

Here, γh\gamma_{h} is the activation threshold, λh∈[0,1]\lambda_{h}\in[0,1] is the intervention strength, and Θt⊕h\Theta_{t}\oplus h denotes temporary application of hh without changing persistent memory. The temporary policy remains a valid action distribution because Eq. (4) is a convex combination of two valid policies.

Verifier-grounded probes.

For a candidate hypothesis hh, FGSE constructs a target-transfer set 𝒯⁡(h)\mathcal{T}(h), a falsification set ℱ⁡(h)\mathcal{F}(h), and a regression set ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h):

𝒫⁡(h)=𝒯⁡(h)∪ℱ⁡(h)∪ℛ⁡(h).\mathcal{P}(h)=\mathcal{T}(h)\cup\mathcal{F}(h)\cup\mathcal{R}(h). (5)

The target-transfer set contains cases where the hypothesis is expected to help. The falsification set contains cases designed to expose overgeneralization. The regression set ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h) contains archived cases that the current agent already solves and that must not be degraded. A probe xx is admitted only when Verifiable⁡(x,vh)=1\operatorname{Verifiable}(x,v_{h})=1, ensuring that the gate is based on executable or externally checkable signals. FGSE builds falsification probes from boundary cases, precondition violations, regression cases, and decoys; their construction is described in Appendix A.2.

Temporary evaluation.

FGSE evaluates hh by comparing the original state Θt\Theta_{t} with the temporary state Θt⊕h\Theta_{t}\oplus h on the same probes:

Δh​(x)=Jvh​(Θt⊕h,x)−Jvh​(Θt,x).\Delta_{h}(x)=J_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)-J_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t},x). (6)

A positive Δh​(x)\Delta_{h}(x) means that the hypothesis improves verifier-grounded performance on xx, while a negative value indicates harm. Empirical estimation under repeated rollouts is given in Appendix A.4.

Let Eh​(Θ,x)∈{0,1}E_{h}(\Theta,x)\in\{0,1\} denote whether the expected effect ehe_{h} is satisfied under state Θ\Theta on task xx. FGSE computes

G^​(h)\displaystyle\widehat{G}(h) =1|𝒯⁡(h)|​∑x∈𝒯⁡(h)Δh​(x),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{T}(h)}\Delta_{h}(x), (7)
P^fail​(h)\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) =1|ℱ⁡(h)|∑x∈ℱ⁡(h)𝕀[Δh(x)<−ϵ∨Eh(Θt⊕h,x)=0],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{F}(h)}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\Delta_{h}(x)<-\epsilon\vee E_{h}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)=0\right],
D^reg​(h)\displaystyle\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h) =1|ℛ⁡(h)|​∑x∈ℛ⁡(h)[−Δh​(x)]+.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{R}(h)}[-\Delta_{h}(x)]_{+}.

Here, ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 is the tolerated verifier-score drop and [⋅]+=max⁡(⋅,0)[\cdot]_{+}=\max(\cdot,0). The three statistics measure useful transfer, targeted falsification risk, and regression damage.

Commitment gate.

The commitment decision is

𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗆𝗂𝗍(h)=𝕀[G^(h)≥η∧P^fail(h)≤δ∧D^reg(h)≤β],\mathsf{Commit}(h)=\mathbb{I}\left[\widehat{G}(h)\geq\eta\wedge\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta\wedge\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta\right], (8)

where η>0\eta>0 is the minimum target-transfer gain, δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1] is the maximum falsification rate, and β≥0\beta\geq 0 is the maximum regression damage. If G^​(h)≥η\widehat{G}(h)\geq\eta but failures are concentrated outside a separable sub-scope, FGSE performs one precondition-refinement pass and reevaluates the refined hypothesis. The refinement objective and separability criterion are given in Appendix A.3. A hypothesis that fails after refinement is rejected.

The persistent state is updated by

Θt+1={Θt⊕h,𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗆𝗂𝗍⁡(h)=1,Θt,𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗆𝗂𝗍⁡(h)=0.\Theta_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\Theta_{t}\oplus h,&\mathsf{Commit}(h)=1,\\ \Theta_{t},&\mathsf{Commit}(h)=0.\end{cases} (9)

A committed hypothesis is stored together with its precondition, behavior change, verifier, evaluated probes, verifier outcomes, and post-commit violation record. Rejected hypotheses are excluded from retrievable memory.

4.3 Runtime Use and Monitoring

During future inference, FGSE retrieves committed hypotheses whose preconditions match the current interaction state and whose violation records remain below threshold. Activated hypotheses modify the policy through the same behavior-transformation interface as Eq. (4). When multiple hypotheses are active, FGSE combines them by normalized precondition scores while preserving a nonzero base-policy contribution. Post-commit violations update a running violation score; hypotheses exceeding the violation threshold are removed from retrieval. The retrieval, combination, and monitoring rules are provided in Appendix A.5.

5 Theoretical Analysis

We analyze whether a hypothesis that passes the finite-probe commitment gate is reliable on the underlying target, falsification, and regression probe distributions. Fix a round tt and condition on the pre-evaluation history, so the current state Θt\Theta_{t}, evidence packet, and finite candidate set ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} are fixed. If scope refinement is used, refinement is performed on a development split, while final commitment uses fresh probes.

For each h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t}, let 𝒟T​(h)\mathcal{D}_{T}(h), 𝒟F​(h)\mathcal{D}_{F}(h), and 𝒟R​(h)\mathcal{D}_{R}(h) denote the target-transfer, falsification, and regression probe distributions. We define

G⁡(h)\displaystyle G(h) =𝔼x∼𝒟T​(h)​[Δh​(x)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{T}(h)}\left[\Delta_{h}(x)\right], (10)
Pfail​(h)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) =ℙx∼𝒟F​(h)[Δh(x)<−ϵ∨Eh(Θt⊕h,x)=0],\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{F}(h)}\left[\Delta_{h}(x)<-\epsilon\ \vee\ E_{h}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)=0\right],
Dreg​(h)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h) =𝔼x∼𝒟R​(h)​[[−Δh​(x)]+].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{R}(h)}\left[[-\Delta_{h}(x)]_{+}\right].

These quantities measure useful transfer, falsification risk, and regression damage, respectively. Let LCBT​(h)\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h), UCBF​(h)\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h), and UCBR​(h)\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h) be one-sided confidence bounds for these three quantities, computed from fresh final probes using empirical-Bernstein bounds for real-valued gains and Bernoulli-KL bounds for falsification events. Their finite-sample forms are given in Appendix B.2.

Theorem 1 (Generalization of the confidence-gated commitment rule).

Suppose that, conditional on the pre-evaluation history, the final probes for each h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} are sampled from 𝒟T​(h)\mathcal{D}_{T}(h), 𝒟F​(h)\mathcal{D}_{F}(h), and 𝒟R​(h)\mathcal{D}_{R}(h). Then, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, all h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} simultaneously satisfy

G⁡(h)≥LCBT​(h),Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h),Dreg​(h)≤UCBR​(h).G(h)\geq\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h),\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h),\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h). (11)

Consequently, any hypothesis satisfying

LCBT​(h)≥η,UCBF​(h)≤δ,UCBR​(h)≤β\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h)\geq\eta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h)\leq\beta (12)

also satisfies the population constraints

G⁡(h)≥η,Pfail​(h)≤δ,Dreg​(h)≤β.G(h)\geq\eta,\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta. (13)

Proof sketch.

Conditioning on the pre-evaluation history fixes ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} and prevents final probes from being reused for hypothesis construction. Empirical-Bernstein inequalities control the bounded target-transfer and regression quantities, while a Bernoulli-KL bound controls falsification risk. A union bound over hypotheses and statistics gives the simultaneous high-probability event, under which the confidence-gated rule implies the corresponding population constraints.

Corollary 1 (Probe complexity of safe commitment).

Up to logarithmic factors in |ℋt||\mathcal{H}_{t}|, 1/α1/\alpha, and the number of falsification probes, it suffices to use

nT=O~​(1ζT2),nR=O~​(1ζR2),nF=O~​(1kl(δ−∥δ))n_{T}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{\zeta_{T}^{2}}\right),\qquad n_{R}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{\zeta_{R}^{2}}\right),\qquad n_{F}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{kl}(\delta_{-}\|\delta)}\right) (14)

final target, regression, and falsification probes to ensure that any hypothesis with empirical target margin ζT\zeta_{T}, empirical regression margin ζR\zeta_{R}, and empirical falsification rate at most δ−<δ\delta_{-}<\delta satisfies G⁡(h)≥ηG(h)\geq\eta, Pfail​(h)≤δP_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta, and Dreg​(h)≤βD_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. The exact finite-sample statement is proved in Appendix B.7.

6 Experiments

6.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets. We evaluate FGSE on verifier-grounded agentic tasks where updates can be tested before persistent commitment. The benchmark suite covers web and browser control with WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) and BrowserGym (Le Sellier de Chezelles et al., 2025), app and API interaction with AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) and τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024), adversarial tool-use robustness with AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024), and long-term memory reliability with LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) and LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024). We also include verifier-rich coding and reasoning diagnostics on HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Details are provided in App. C.

Evaluation metrics. We report each benchmark’s official task metric, including success rate, task-goal completion, pass rate or passk\mathrm{pass}^{k}, utility and security success, QA accuracy/F1, pass@1, resolved rate, and exact-match accuracy. To evaluate safe self-evolution, we additionally report target-transfer gain G^\widehat{G}, falsification failure rate P^fail\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}, regression damage D^reg\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}, post-commit violation rate, and harmful update rate.

Baselines. We compare FGSE with non-evolving agents, including direct prompting and ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), as well as self-update baselines such as Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Voyager-style skill memory (Wang et al., 2023), and naive episodic memory. We further compare with recent self-evolving or agent-optimization methods, including Symbolic Learning (Zhou et al., 2025), AlphaLLM (Tian et al., 2024), GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025a), ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), MetaAgent (Zhang et al., 2025b), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), Lighthouse (Yang et al., 2025), and ACE (Zhang et al., 2026f). For methods requiring workflow search, external data, or model updates, we separate controlled comparisons from native-setting results, since FGSE modifies only the persistent agent state and commitment rule.

Implementation details. The default backbone is a ReAct-style executor with persistent memory retrieval. FGSE proposes at most B=3B=3 candidate hypotheses per episode and evaluates each using target-transfer, falsification, and regression probes with default budgets |𝒯⁡(h)|=8|\mathcal{T}(h)|=8, |ℱ⁡(h)|=16|\mathcal{F}(h)|=16, and |ℛ⁡(h)|=16|\mathcal{R}(h)|=16. We tune only η\eta, δ\delta, and β\beta on the development split, using defaults η=0.03\eta=0.03, δ=0.05\delta=0.05, β=0.01\beta=0.01, ϵ=0\epsilon=0, γh=0.5\gamma_{h}=0.5, and λh=0.8\lambda_{h}=0.8. Stochastic settings use three random seeds, and we report mean performance with bootstrap confidence intervals. Refer to App. C for more details.

6.2 Main Results

Overall comparison.

Table 1 shows that FGSE improves over memory-writing and reflection-style baselines across verifier-rich web, app, tool-use, and memory benchmarks. The gains are especially clear on verifier-rich settings such as WebArena, AppWorld, and τ\tau-bench, where tool-state and database-state validators provide reliable evidence for pre-commitment testing. Appendix D.1 further shows that FGSE improves long-term memory reliability while reducing falsification failures, regression damage, and harmful committed updates.

Domain-level update diagnostics. Beyond task success, Figure 4 reports update-centric metrics across domains, including G^\widehat{G}, P^fail\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}, D^reg\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}, and harmful update rate. AppWorld, τ\tau-bench, AgentDojo, and long-term memory benchmarks show both meaningful gains and higher safety risks, indicating greater vulnerability to overgeneralized self-updates. Coding and math tasks exhibit lower falsification and regression risks due to cleaner executable or exact-match verifiers, while SWE-bench remains regression-prone because repository-level changes are highly contextual. These results support verifier-grounded falsification over commitment based only on target improvement.

6.3 Ablation and Mechanism Analysis

Single-factor ablation.

We isolate FGSE components by removing or replacing one component at a time and report both task performance and update reliability. Blue values in parentheses denote absolute changes from full FGSE, with negative values indicating drops for higher-is-better metrics and positive values indicating worse lower-is-better metrics. Tables 2 and 6 show that each component contributes. Removing structured hypotheses causes the largest drop, reducing WebArena SR by 4.24.2 points, AppWorld Avg. by 5.95.9 points, and LoCoMo Avg. R-L by 4.784.78 points, confirming the need for scoped, verifier-aware updates. Target-transfer probes improve useful generalization, as G^\widehat{G} drops from 12.9%12.9\% to 9.8%9.8\% without them, while falsification probes prevent unsafe overgeneralization, with P^fail\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}} increasing from 5.0%5.0\% to 18.6%18.6\% and harmful updates from 3.6%3.6\% to 10.6%10.6\% when removed. The regression archive reduces D^reg\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}} from 5.2%5.2\% to 1.3%1.3\%, and scope refinement, post-commit monitoring, and executable verifiers further improve the transfer-safety trade-off.

Transferability of candidate updates.

We assess whether episode-derived updates capture reusable rules that transfer beyond the triggering case. We therefore evaluate each candidate before commitment using three temporary statistics: target-transfer gain G^​(h)\widehat{G}(h), falsification failure rate P^fail​(h)\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h), and regression damage D^reg​(h)\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h). Figure 5(a) plots candidates in a Transfer–Falsification volcano plot, with G^​(h)\widehat{G}(h) on the xx-axis, −log10⁡(P^fail​(h)+ϵ0)-\log_{10}(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)+\epsilon_{0}) on the yy-axis, point size encoding D^reg​(h)\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h), and color indicating the gate decision. The plot reveals three groups: committed updates in the upper right with high transfer and low risk, unsafe shortcuts in the lower right, and safe but low-transfer local fixes in the upper left. In this run, FGSE commits 104/380104/380 candidates, achieving average G^=10.77%\widehat{G}=10.77\%, P^fail=1.28%\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}=1.28\%, and D^reg=0.60%\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}=0.60\%. The 101101 rejected candidates that exceed the gain threshold η\eta show much higher falsification and regression risk, with P^fail=22.82%\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}=22.82\% and D^reg=4.85%\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}=4.85\%. Refined candidates lie between these groups, suggesting that many useful but unsafe updates require scope narrowing before commitment.

Commit–refine–reject decision boundary. To examine the gate, we map each candidate into a simplex over normalized target gain, falsification risk, and regression damage. For each candidate hh, we normalize the three statistics across candidates and project them onto simplex coordinates (gh,fh,rh)(g_{h},f_{h},r_{h}) with gh+fh+rh=1g_{h}+f_{h}+r_{h}=1. Figure 5(b) shows the joint role of the three statistics: commit lies in the high-gain, low-risk region, reject concentrates near the high-risk, high-regression edge, and refine forms a transition band between them. This pattern indicates that FGSE performs structured triage, committing gain-dominant updates, refining repairable but ambiguous ones, and rejecting risk-dominant candidates.

7 Conclusion

We studied reliable self-evolution for long-horizon LLM agents, focusing on when episode-derived lessons should enter persistent memory. FGSE treats each candidate update as a structured, verifier-grounded hypothesis and commits it only after target-transfer, falsification, and regression testing. Our results show that safe adaptation requires evaluating usefulness, boundary failures, and regression on previously solved behavior alongside source-task improvement. Future work can extend falsification-gated update control to multimodal agents (Xu et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026e; Kang et al., 2026), collaborative tool-use systems (Fan et al., 2026), and settings where verifiers must be learned or approximated.

Appendix A Additional Technical Details

A.1 Details of the Exploratory Preliminary Study

The preliminary study in Section 3 examines naive episode-derived memory writing. The agent directly summarizes a completed episode into a free-form lesson and writes it into persistent memory.

Episode-derived lessons.

For each completed episode, the base agent observes the task instruction xx, its interaction trajectory τ\tau, and the verifier outcome rr. It then produces a natural-language lesson

u=SummarizeLesson⁡(x,τ,r),u=\mathrm{SummarizeLesson}(x,\tau,r), (15)

which may take the form of a rule, reminder, correction, or behavioral heuristic. The updated agent state is obtained by simply appending uu to the memory context:

Θ⊕u=(ℳ∪{u},π),\Theta\oplus u=(\mathcal{M}\cup\{u\},\pi), (16)

where ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes the current memory and π\pi denotes the unchanged base policy. This direct memory-writing procedure is a common self-improvement baseline that exposes unsafe updates.

Probe groups.

To analyze the effect of a lesson uu, we evaluate the original agent Θ\Theta and the memory-augmented agent Θ⊕u\Theta\oplus u on four groups of diagnostic cases. The source-replay group 𝒞src​(u)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{src}}(u) contains the original episode and minor perturbations that preserve the same intended solution. The near-transfer group 𝒞near​(u)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{near}}(u) contains tasks that share the same underlying behavioral pattern but differ in surface form, entities, or context. The boundary-contrast group 𝒞bdry​(u)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{bdry}}(u) contains cases that are superficially similar to the source episode but should not trigger the same lesson. The archived-success group 𝒞arch​(u)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{arch}}(u) contains previously solved cases sampled from the agent’s historical archive. The first two groups measure whether the lesson captures a useful pattern, while the latter two groups measure whether it overgeneralizes or interferes with existing behavior.

Verifier-score changes.

For a case xx, we estimate the verifier-grounded performance of an agent state Θ\Theta as

J(Θ,x)=1L∑ℓ=1Lv(x,τ(ℓ)),τ(ℓ)∼pΘ(⋅∣x),J(\Theta,x)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}v(x,\tau^{(\ell)}),\qquad\tau^{(\ell)}\sim p_{\Theta}(\cdot\mid x), (17)

where v⁡(x,τ)∈[0,1]v(x,\tau)\in[0,1] is the task verifier and LL is the number of repeated rollouts. For deterministic tasks, L=1L=1 is sufficient. The effect of lesson uu on a case group 𝒞\mathcal{C} is

Δ𝒞​(u)=1|𝒞|​∑x∈𝒞[J⁡(Θ⊕u,x)−J⁡(Θ,x)].\Delta_{\mathcal{C}}(u)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\left[J(\Theta\oplus u,x)-J(\Theta,x)\right]. (18)

We report source gain Δsrc​(u)\Delta_{\mathrm{src}}(u), near-transfer gain Δnear​(u)\Delta_{\mathrm{near}}(u), boundary harm

Hbdry​(u)=[−Δ𝒞bdry​(u)]+,H_{\mathrm{bdry}}(u)=\left[-\Delta_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{bdry}}}(u)\right]_{+}, (19)

and archive harm

Harch​(u)=[−Δ𝒞arch​(u)]+.H_{\mathrm{arch}}(u)=\left[-\Delta_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{arch}}}(u)\right]_{+}. (20)

A lesson is considered locally useful if it improves near-transfer cases, but it is considered unsafe if it also induces large boundary or archive harm.

Scope-specificity annotation.

To understand why some useful lessons are harmful, we annotate each free-form lesson with a coarse scope-specificity score s⁡(u)∈[0,1]s(u)\in[0,1]. A lesson receives a higher score when it contains explicit applicability conditions, contextual triggers, exception clauses, or task-specific constraints. It receives a lower score when it is phrased as a broad heuristic without clear conditions. This analysis-only score tests whether overgeneralization is associated with underspecified lesson scope; update selection in the preliminary study proceeds without it.

Sequential memory-writing analysis.

To study error accumulation, we simulate sequential memory writing over a stream of candidate lessons. After writing kk lessons, the agent state is

Θk=Θ0⊕{u1,…,uk},\Theta_{k}=\Theta_{0}\oplus\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\}, (21)

and its held-out verifier score is measured on a fixed evaluation set ℰ\mathcal{E}:

Sk=1|ℰ|​∑x∈ℰJ⁡(Θk,x).S_{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{E}}J(\Theta_{k},x). (22)

We compare three diagnostic memory-writing strategies: writing all lessons, writing only lessons that improve the source episode, and a hindsight safe subset. The hindsight subset keeps lessons with high near-transfer gain and low boundary/archive harm, and is used only as an oracle diagnostic upper bound. It is not available to the agent during deployment. This comparison isolates the main observation that source improvement alone is insufficient for stable long-term self-evolution.

Post-hoc scope localization.

For lessons that are useful but harmful, we conduct a post-hoc localization analysis. Given a lesson uu with positive near-transfer gain but high boundary harm, we inspect the boundary failures and rewrite the lesson into a narrower version u′u^{\prime} by adding an explicit applicability condition. We then reevaluate u′u^{\prime} on the same near-transfer and boundary-contrast groups. We summarize the effect of localization by the transfer-retention ratio

Rretain​(u′)=Δnear​(u′)Δnear​(u)+ε,R_{\mathrm{retain}}(u^{\prime})=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{near}}(u^{\prime})}{\Delta_{\mathrm{near}}(u)+\varepsilon}, (23)

and the boundary-harm reduction ratio

Rreduce​(u′)=Hbdry​(u)−Hbdry​(u′)Hbdry​(u)+ε,R_{\mathrm{reduce}}(u^{\prime})=\frac{H_{\mathrm{bdry}}(u)-H_{\mathrm{bdry}}(u^{\prime})}{H_{\mathrm{bdry}}(u)+\varepsilon}, (24)

where ε\varepsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. This separate diagnostic motivates explicit applicability conditions and refinement of useful but overly broad candidates in the main method.

Connection to the method.

The preliminary study supports three design choices. First, testing episode-derived updates before persistence can expose unsafe free-form lessons. Second, contrastive and archived cases expose boundary failures that source or near-transfer cases can miss. Third, scope refinement can repair some harmful lessons while retaining their useful content. These observations motivate the structured hypothesis representation, temporary evaluation, verifier-grounded commitment, and scope refinement introduced in Section 4.

A.2 Verifier-Grounded Probe Construction

FGSE constructs probes from three candidate sources: archived solved tasks, verifier-preserving perturbations of the triggering episode, and language-model-generated candidates filtered by executable verifiers. The verifier filter is applied before evaluation:

Verifiable(x,vh)=1⟺vh(x,τ)returns a stable score for every evaluated rollout τ.\operatorname{Verifiable}(x,v_{h})=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_{h}(x,\tau)\ \text{returns a stable score for every evaluated rollout }\tau. (25)

Tasks that cannot be checked by vhv_{h} are excluded from the gate.

The falsification set is decomposed as

ℱ⁡(h)=ℱbd​(h)∪ℱpv​(h)∪ℱrg​(h)∪ℱdc​(h).\mathcal{F}(h)=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{bd}}(h)\cup\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pv}}(h)\cup\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{rg}}(h)\cup\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{dc}}(h). (26)

Here, ℱbd\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{bd}} contains boundary probes near the activation threshold of chc_{h}, ℱpv\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pv}} contains precondition-violation probes that are similar to the claimed scope but should not activate the rule, ℱrg\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{rg}} contains regression probes from previously solved cases, and ℱdc\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{dc}} contains decoy probes that are superficially similar to target cases but require different behavior.

For each probe type q∈{bd,pv,rg,dc}q\in\{\mathrm{bd},\mathrm{pv},\mathrm{rg},\mathrm{dc}\}, FGSE assigns a risk score

ρq​(x,h)={exp(−|ch(x)−γh|/σ),q=bd,(1−ch​(x))​sim⁡(x,h),q=pv,𝕀[Jvh(Θt,x)≥ζ]sim(x,h),q=rg,sim(x,h)𝕀[ch(x)<γh],q=dc.\rho_{q}(x;h)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\left(-|c_{h}(x)-\gamma_{h}|/\sigma\right),&q=\mathrm{bd},\\[2.0pt] (1-c_{h}(x))\,\operatorname{sim}(x,h),&q=\mathrm{pv},\\[2.0pt] \mathbb{I}[J_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t},x)\geq\zeta]\,\operatorname{sim}(x,h),&q=\mathrm{rg},\\[2.0pt] \operatorname{sim}(x,h)\,\mathbb{I}[c_{h}(x)<\gamma_{h}],&q=\mathrm{dc}.\end{cases} (27)

In Eq. (27), σ>0\sigma>0 controls the width of the boundary region, sim⁡(x,h)\operatorname{sim}(x,h) measures semantic or structural similarity between xx and the triggering context of hh, and ζ\zeta is the score threshold for considering an archived case solved.

The selected probes are

ℱq​(h)=TopKx∈𝒳q⁡{ρq​(x,h):Verifiable⁡(x,vh)=1},\mathcal{F}_{q}(h)=\operatorname{TopK}_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{q}}\left\{\rho_{q}(x;h):\operatorname{Verifiable}(x,v_{h})=1\right\}, (28)

where 𝒳q\mathcal{X}_{q} is the candidate pool for probe type qq. Boundary probes test whether the hypothesis changes behavior too aggressively near its activation threshold. Precondition-violation probes test whether the rule fires outside its intended condition. Regression probes measure damage to cases already solved by Θt\Theta_{t}. Decoy probes test whether superficial similarity causes the wrong behavior change.

The target-transfer set 𝒯⁡(h)\mathcal{T}(h) is selected from verifiable candidates satisfying ch​(x)≥γhc_{h}(x)\geq\gamma_{h}. FGSE prioritizes candidates that match the precondition while differing from the triggering task in surface form, tool trace, or problem instance. This tests transfer beyond memorization of the original episode.

A.3 Precondition Refinement

Refinement is used when a hypothesis improves target probes but fails on falsification probes that can be separated by a more precise precondition. FGSE forms the safe and falsifying sets

𝒫h+\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{h}^{+} ={x∈𝒯(h)∪ℱ(h):Δh(x)≥0,Eh(Θt⊕h,x)=1},\displaystyle=\{x\in\mathcal{T}(h)\cup\mathcal{F}(h):\Delta_{h}(x)\geq 0,\ E_{h}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)=1\},
𝒫h−\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{h}^{-} ={x∈ℱ⁡(h):Δh​(x)<−ϵ∨Eh​(Θt⊕h,x)=0}.\displaystyle=\{x\in\mathcal{F}(h):\Delta_{h}(x)<-\epsilon\ \vee\ E_{h}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)=0\}. (29)

The refined precondition is obtained by

ch′=arg⁡minc∈ℭ​[Ω⁡(c)+λ+​∑x∈𝒫h+ℓ⁡(1,c⁡(x))+λ−​∑x∈𝒫h−ℓ⁡(0,c⁡(x))].c_{h}^{\prime}=\arg\min_{c\in\mathfrak{C}}\left[\Omega(c)+\lambda_{+}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}_{h}^{+}}\ell(1,c(x))+\lambda_{-}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}_{h}^{-}}\ell(0,c(x))\right]. (30)

Here, ℭ\mathfrak{C} is the precondition class, Ω⁡(c)\Omega(c) penalizes overly complex conditions, ℓ\ell is binary cross-entropy, and λ+,λ−≥0\lambda_{+},\lambda_{-}\geq 0 weight safe and falsifying probes.

FGSE triggers refinement only when the following separability score is below a threshold:

Sep(h)=minc∈ℭ[1|𝒫h+|∑x∈𝒫h+𝕀[c(x)<γh]+1|𝒫h−|∑x∈𝒫h−𝕀[c(x)≥γh]]≤αsep.\operatorname{Sep}(h)=\min_{c\in\mathfrak{C}}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{h}^{+}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}_{h}^{+}}\mathbb{I}[c(x)<\gamma_{h}]+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{h}^{-}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}_{h}^{-}}\mathbb{I}[c(x)\geq\gamma_{h}]\right]\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}. (31)

A refined hypothesis is h′=(ch′,bh,eh,vh)h^{\prime}=(c_{h}^{\prime},b_{h},e_{h},v_{h}). FGSE performs one refinement pass. The refined hypothesis is then evaluated by the same equations used in the main method. If it fails the gate after refinement, it is rejected.

A.4 Empirical Estimation Under Stochastic Rollouts

The verifier-grounded score in Eq. (2) is estimated with repeated rollouts:

J^v(Θ,x)=1n∑j=1nv(x,τ(j)),τ(j)∼pΘ(⋅∣x).\widehat{J}_{v}(\Theta,x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}v(x,\tau^{(j)}),\qquad\tau^{(j)}\sim p_{\Theta}(\cdot\mid x). (32)

The empirical update effect is

Δ^h​(x)=J^vh​(Θt⊕h,x)−J^vh​(Θt,x).\widehat{\Delta}_{h}(x)=\widehat{J}_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)-\widehat{J}_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t},x). (33)

In experiments with deterministic verifiers and deterministic decoding, n=1n=1 is sufficient. With stochastic decoding or nondeterministic tool responses, FGSE uses paired random seeds for Θt\Theta_{t} and Θt⊕h\Theta_{t}\oplus h when the environment supports seed control. This reduces variance in Δ^h​(x)\widehat{\Delta}_{h}(x) because both states are evaluated under matched rollout conditions.

For finite probe budgets, FGSE reports the conservative falsification score

Sfail(h)=P^fail(h)+κ|ℱ(h)|−1/2,S_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)=\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)+\kappa|\mathcal{F}(h)|^{-1/2}, (34)

where κ≥0\kappa\geq 0 controls the penalty for small falsification sets. This score is used for analysis and ablations. The main gate in Eq. (8) uses the empirical falsification rate P^fail​(h)\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h).

A.5 Runtime Retrieval, Combination, and Monitoring

At inference time, FGSE retrieves committed hypotheses whose preconditions match the current interaction state z=(x,τ<ℓ)z=(x,\tau_{<\ell}):

ℋt(z)={h∈ℳt:ch(z)≥γh,ut(h)≤umax},\mathcal{H}_{t}(z)=\{h\in\mathcal{M}_{t}:c_{h}(z)\geq\gamma_{h},\ u_{t}(h)\leq u_{\max}\}, (35)

where ut​(h)u_{t}(h) is the post-commit violation score and umaxu_{\max} is the maximum allowed violation level.

When ℋt​(z)\mathcal{H}_{t}(z) is nonempty, FGSE assigns normalized weights

wh​(z)=exp⁡(ch​(z)/ρ)∑h′∈ℋt​(z)exp⁡(ch′​(z)/ρ),h∈ℋt​(z),w_{h}(z)=\frac{\exp(c_{h}(z)/\rho)}{\sum_{h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}(z)}\exp(c_{h^{\prime}}(z)/\rho)},\qquad h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}(z), (36)

where ρ>0\rho>0 is the temperature. The runtime policy is

πtFGSE​(a∣z)=(1−λ⁡(z))​πΘt​(a∣z)+λ⁡(z)​∑h∈ℋt​(z)wh​(z)​bh​[πΘt]​(a∣z),\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{FGSE}}(a\mid z)=(1-\lambda(z))\pi_{\Theta_{t}}(a\mid z)+\lambda(z)\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}(z)}w_{h}(z)b_{h}[\pi_{\Theta_{t}}](a\mid z), (37)

where λ⁡(z)∈[0,1]\lambda(z)\in[0,1] is the total intervention strength. This form preserves a nonzero base-policy contribution even when several hypotheses are active.

After a committed hypothesis is activated, FGSE records whether its expected effect is violated:

Vt(h,xt)=𝕀[Eh(Θt,xt)=0∨Jvh(Θt,xt)<ζh],V_{t}(h,x_{t})=\mathbb{I}\left[E_{h}(\Theta_{t},x_{t})=0\vee J_{v_{h}}(\Theta_{t},x_{t})<\zeta_{h}\right], (38)

where ζh\zeta_{h} is the minimum acceptable verifier score associated with hypothesis hh. The violation score is updated by

ut+1​(h)=ρu​ut​(h)+(1−ρu)​Vt​(h,xt),u_{t+1}(h)=\rho_{u}u_{t}(h)+(1-\rho_{u})V_{t}(h,x_{t}), (39)

where ρu∈[0,1)\rho_{u}\in[0,1) controls the memory of previous violations. If ut+1​(h)>umaxu_{t+1}(h)>u_{\max}, the hypothesis is removed from the active retrieval set. Removed hypotheses remain in the audit archive and are not used for future action selection.

A.6 Audit Record

Each committed hypothesis is stored with an audit record

Record⁡(h)=(h,𝒯⁡(h),ℱ⁡(h),ℛ⁡(h),{Δh​(x)}x∈𝒫⁡(h),G^​(h),P^fail​(h),D^reg​(h),ut​(h)).\operatorname{Record}(h)=\left(h,\mathcal{T}(h),\mathcal{F}(h),\mathcal{R}(h),\{\Delta_{h}(x)\}_{x\in\mathcal{P}(h)},\widehat{G}(h),\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h),\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h),u_{t}(h)\right). (40)

The audit record supports post-hoc inspection of why a rule was committed, which probes were used to falsify it, and whether the rule later accumulated violations.

A.7 Detailed Algorithm with Refinement

Practical representation of hypotheses.

In implementation, each hypothesis is stored as a schema-constrained JSON object. The precondition field is a natural-language predicate together with a scoring function implemented by a lightweight LLM classifier or rule-based matcher. The behavior field specifies a bounded prompt/tool-policy patch. The expected-effect field specifies a verifier-observable condition, and the verifier field points to the benchmark validator or executable checker. Audits of synthetic healthcare workflows also expose escalation errors under conflicting evidence and brittle routing rules under unseen paraphrases [Zheng et al., 2026].

Appendix B Proofs for the Commitment Gate Generalization

B.1 Conditional Setup

We prove Theorem 1 and Corollary 1. Fix a round tt. Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} denote the sigma-field containing the current agent state Θt\Theta_{t}, the evidence packet, the audit archive, the proposal and refinement randomness before final evaluation, and the finite candidate set ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}. Throughout the proof, we condition on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. Thus, the candidate set is fixed before the final evaluation probes are sampled.

For each h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t}, define the target-transfer random variable

XhT=Δh​(x),x∼𝒟T​(h).X^{T}_{h}=\Delta_{h}(x),\qquad x\sim\mathcal{D}_{T}(h). (41)

Because verifier scores lie in [0,1][0,1], we have

XhT∈[−1,1].X^{T}_{h}\in[-1,1]. (42)

The population and empirical target-transfer gains are

G⁡(h)=𝔼⁡[XhT],G^​(h)=1nT​∑i=1nTXh,iT.G(h)=\mathbb{E}[X^{T}_{h}],\qquad\widehat{G}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{T}}X^{T}_{h,i}. (43)

The empirical target-transfer variance is

V^T​(h)=1nT​∑i=1nT(Xh,iT−G^​(h))2.\widehat{V}_{T}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{T}}\left(X^{T}_{h,i}-\widehat{G}(h)\right)^{2}. (44)

For falsification probes, define the Bernoulli random variable

XhF=𝕀[Δh(x)<−ϵ∨Eh(Θt⊕h,x)=0],x∼𝒟F(h).X^{F}_{h}=\mathbb{I}\left[\Delta_{h}(x)<-\epsilon\ \vee\ E_{h}(\Theta_{t}\oplus h,x)=0\right],\qquad x\sim\mathcal{D}_{F}(h). (45)

Then

XhF∈{0,1}.X^{F}_{h}\in\{0,1\}. (46)

The population falsification risk and empirical failure rate are

Pfail​(h)=𝔼⁡[XhF],P^fail​(h)=1nF​∑i=1nFXh,iF.P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)=\mathbb{E}[X^{F}_{h}],\qquad\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{F}}X^{F}_{h,i}. (47)

For regression probes, define

XhR=[−Δh​(x)]+,x∼𝒟R​(h).X^{R}_{h}=[-\Delta_{h}(x)]_{+},\qquad x\sim\mathcal{D}_{R}(h). (48)

Since Δh​(x)∈[−1,1]\Delta_{h}(x)\in[-1,1], we have

XhR∈[0,1].X^{R}_{h}\in[0,1]. (49)

The population and empirical regression damages are

Dreg​(h)=𝔼⁡[XhR],D^reg​(h)=1nR​∑i=1nRXh,iR.D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)=\mathbb{E}[X^{R}_{h}],\qquad\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{R}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{R}}X^{R}_{h,i}. (50)

The empirical regression variance is

V^R​(h)=1nR​∑i=1nR(Xh,iR−D^reg​(h))2.\widehat{V}_{R}(h)=\frac{1}{n_{R}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{R}}\left(X^{R}_{h,i}-\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\right)^{2}. (51)

The analysis treats the randomness in XhTX^{T}_{h}, XhFX^{F}_{h}, and XhRX^{R}_{h} as including both probe sampling and any rollout randomness used to estimate verifier outcomes. The only properties needed are boundedness and conditional independence of the final evaluation samples for each fixed hh.

B.2 Confidence Bounds Used by the Commitment Gate

Let nT,nF,nRn_{T},n_{F},n_{R} be the numbers of final target, falsification, and regression probes. Let αT,αF,αR>0\alpha_{T},\alpha_{F},\alpha_{R}>0 satisfy

αT+αF+αR=α.\alpha_{T}+\alpha_{F}+\alpha_{R}=\alpha. (52)

Define the logarithmic factors

LT=log⁡2​|ℋt|αT,LR=log⁡2​|ℋt|αR,LF=log⁡(nF+1)​|ℋt|αF.L_{T}=\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{T}},\qquad L_{R}=\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{R}},\qquad L_{F}=\log\frac{(n_{F}+1)|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{F}}. (53)

The empirical-Bernstein slacks are

εT​(h)=2​V^T​(h)​LTnT+14​LT3​(nT−1),εR​(h)=2​V^R​(h)​LRnR+7​LR3​(nR−1).\varepsilon_{T}(h)=\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{T}(h)L_{T}}{n_{T}}}+\frac{14L_{T}}{3(n_{T}-1)},\qquad\varepsilon_{R}(h)=\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{R}(h)L_{R}}{n_{R}}}+\frac{7L_{R}}{3(n_{R}-1)}. (54)

The target lower confidence bound and regression upper confidence bound are

LCBT​(h)=G^​(h)−εT​(h),UCBR​(h)=D^reg​(h)+εR​(h).\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h)=\widehat{G}(h)-\varepsilon_{T}(h),\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h)=\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)+\varepsilon_{R}(h). (55)

For p,q∈[0,1]p,q\in[0,1], define the binary KL divergence

kl(p∥q)=plogpq+(1−p)log1−p1−q,\mathrm{kl}(p\|q)=p\log\frac{p}{q}+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}, (56)

with the standard continuous extension at the boundary. The KL upper confidence bound for falsification risk is

UCBF(h)=sup{q∈[P^fail(h),1]:kl(P^fail(h)∥q)≤LFnF}.\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h)=\sup\left\{q\in[\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h),1]:\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|q\right)\leq\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}\right\}. (57)

B.3 Concentration Tools

We use two concentration results. The first controls bounded real-valued random variables using empirical variance.

Lemma 1 (One-sided empirical Bernstein inequality).

Let Y1,…,YnY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} be independent random variables taking values in an interval of length 𝔟\mathfrak{b}. Let

μ=𝔼⁡[Y1],μ^=1n​∑i=1nYi,\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y_{1}],\qquad\widehat{\mu}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_{i}, (58)

and

V^=1n​∑i=1n(Yi−μ^)2.\widehat{V}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu})^{2}. (59)

For any ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and n≥2n\geq 2, with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

μ−μ^≤2​V^​log⁡(2/ρ)n+7​𝔟​log⁡(2/ρ)3​(n−1).\mu-\widehat{\mu}\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}\log(2/\rho)}{n}}+\frac{7\mathfrak{b}\log(2/\rho)}{3(n-1)}. (60)

The same inequality also holds with μ^−μ\widehat{\mu}-\mu on the left-hand side.

Proof.

This is the standard one-sided form of the empirical Bernstein inequality for bounded random variables. The lower-tail statement follows by applying the same result to −Yi-Y_{i}, whose range length remains 𝔟\mathfrak{b}. ∎

The second result gives a KL confidence bound for Bernoulli variables.

Lemma 2 (Bernoulli KL confidence bound).

Let B1,…,BnB_{1},\ldots,B_{n} be i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with mean pp, and let

p^=1n​∑i=1nBi.\widehat{p}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{i}. (61)

Then, for any u>0u>0,

ℙ(kl(p^∥p)≥u)≤(n+1)exp(−nu).\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{kl}(\widehat{p}\|p)\geq u\right)\leq(n+1)\exp(-nu). (62)
Proof.

For each k∈{0,1,…,n}k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}, let

qk=kn.q_{k}=\frac{k}{n}. (63)

The event p^=qk\widehat{p}=q_{k} has probability

ℙ⁡(p^=qk)=(nk)​pk​(1−p)n−k.\mathbb{P}(\widehat{p}=q_{k})=\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}. (64)

Using the type-counting bound

(nk)≤exp⁡(n​H​(qk)),\binom{n}{k}\leq\exp\left(nH(q_{k})\right), (65)

where

H⁡(q)=−q​log⁡q−(1−q)​log⁡(1−q),H(q)=-q\log q-(1-q)\log(1-q), (66)

we obtain

ℙ⁡(p^=qk)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\widehat{p}=q_{k}) =(nk)​pn​qk​(1−p)n⁡(1−qk)\displaystyle=\binom{n}{k}p^{nq_{k}}(1-p)^{n(1-q_{k})} (67)
≤exp⁡(n​H​(qk)+n​qk​log⁡p+n⁡(1−qk)​log⁡(1−p))\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(nH(q_{k})+nq_{k}\log p+n(1-q_{k})\log(1-p)\right)
=exp⁡(−n⁡[qk​log⁡qkp+(1−qk)​log⁡1−qk1−p])\displaystyle=\exp\left(-n\left[q_{k}\log\frac{q_{k}}{p}+(1-q_{k})\log\frac{1-q_{k}}{1-p}\right]\right)
=exp(−nkl(qk∥p)).\displaystyle=\exp\left(-n\mathrm{kl}(q_{k}\|p)\right).

Therefore,

ℙ(kl(p^∥p)≥u)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{kl}(\widehat{p}\|p)\geq u\right) =∑k:kl(qk∥p)≥uℙ(p^=qk)\displaystyle=\sum_{k:\mathrm{kl}(q_{k}\|p)\geq u}\mathbb{P}(\widehat{p}=q_{k}) (68)
≤∑k:kl(qk∥p)≥uexp(−nkl(qk∥p))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k:\mathrm{kl}(q_{k}\|p)\geq u}\exp\left(-n\mathrm{kl}(q_{k}\|p)\right)
≤∑k=0nexp⁡(−n​u)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n}\exp(-nu)
=(n+1)​exp⁡(−n​u).\displaystyle=(n+1)\exp(-nu).

This proves the claim. ∎

B.4 Uniform Confidence Event

We now prove that the three confidence bounds hold simultaneously for all hypotheses in ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}.

Lemma 3 (Uniform confidence event).

With probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, every h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} simultaneously satisfies

G⁡(h)≥LCBT​(h),Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h),Dreg​(h)≤UCBR​(h).G(h)\geq\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h),\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h),\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h). (69)
Proof.

We prove the target, regression, and falsification bounds separately and then apply a union bound.

First consider target-transfer gain. For a fixed hh, apply Lemma 1 to XhTX^{T}_{h}. Its range length is

𝔟T=2.\mathfrak{b}_{T}=2. (70)

Set

ρT=αT|ℋt|.\rho_{T}=\frac{\alpha_{T}}{|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}. (71)

Then

log⁡2ρT=log⁡2​|ℋt|αT=LT.\log\frac{2}{\rho_{T}}=\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{T}}=L_{T}. (72)

For this fixed hh, Lemma 1 gives

G​(h)−G^​(h)\displaystyle G(h)-\widehat{G}(h) ≥−[2​V^T​(h)​LTnT+7​𝔟T​LT3​(nT−1)]\displaystyle\geq-\left[\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{T}(h)L_{T}}{n_{T}}}+\frac{7\mathfrak{b}_{T}L_{T}}{3(n_{T}-1)}\right] (73)
=−[2​V^T​(h)​LTnT+14​LT3​(nT−1)]\displaystyle=-\left[\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{T}(h)L_{T}}{n_{T}}}+\frac{14L_{T}}{3(n_{T}-1)}\right]
=−εT​(h).\displaystyle=-\varepsilon_{T}(h).

Thus,

G⁡(h)≥G^​(h)−εT​(h)=LCBT​(h).G(h)\geq\widehat{G}(h)-\varepsilon_{T}(h)=\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h). (74)

A union bound over h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} gives

ℙ(∀h∈ℋt:G(h)≥LCBT(h))≥1−αT.\mathbb{P}\left(\forall h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}:G(h)\geq\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h)\right)\geq 1-\alpha_{T}. (75)

Next consider regression damage. For a fixed hh, apply Lemma 1 to XhRX^{R}_{h}. Its range length is

𝔟R=1.\mathfrak{b}_{R}=1. (76)

Set

ρR=αR|ℋt|.\rho_{R}=\frac{\alpha_{R}}{|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}. (77)

Then

log⁡2ρR=log⁡2​|ℋt|αR=LR.\log\frac{2}{\rho_{R}}=\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{R}}=L_{R}. (78)

For this fixed hh, Lemma 1 gives

Dreg​(h)−D^reg​(h)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)-\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h) ≤2​V^R​(h)​LRnR+7​𝔟R​LR3​(nR−1)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{R}(h)L_{R}}{n_{R}}}+\frac{7\mathfrak{b}_{R}L_{R}}{3(n_{R}-1)} (79)
=2​V^R​(h)​LRnR+7​LR3​(nR−1)\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat{V}_{R}(h)L_{R}}{n_{R}}}+\frac{7L_{R}}{3(n_{R}-1)}
=εR​(h).\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{R}(h).

Therefore,

Dreg​(h)≤D^reg​(h)+εR​(h)=UCBR​(h).D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)+\varepsilon_{R}(h)=\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h). (80)

A union bound over h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} gives

ℙ(∀h∈ℋt:Dreg(h)≤UCBR(h))≥1−αR.\mathbb{P}\left(\forall h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}:D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h)\right)\geq 1-\alpha_{R}. (81)

Finally consider falsification risk. For a fixed hh, apply Lemma 2 to XhFX^{F}_{h}. Let

uF=LFnF.u_{F}=\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}. (82)

Then

ℙ(kl(P^fail(h)∥Pfail(h))>LFnF)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\right)>\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}\right) ≤(nF+1)​exp⁡(−LF)\displaystyle\leq(n_{F}+1)\exp(-L_{F}) (83)
=(nF+1)​exp⁡(−log⁡(nF+1)​|ℋt|αF)\displaystyle=(n_{F}+1)\exp\left(-\log\frac{(n_{F}+1)|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}{\alpha_{F}}\right)
=αF|ℋt|.\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{F}}{|\mathcal{H}_{t}|}.

A union bound over h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} yields

ℙ(∀h∈ℋt:kl(P^fail(h)∥Pfail(h))≤LFnF)≥1−αF.\mathbb{P}\left(\forall h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}:\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\right)\leq\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}\right)\geq 1-\alpha_{F}. (84)

On the event in Eq. (84), we prove that Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h)P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h) for every hh. Fix hh. If Pfail​(h)≤P^fail​(h)P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h), then

Pfail​(h)≤P^fail​(h)≤UCBF​(h),P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h), (85)

because q=P^fail​(h)q=\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) is feasible in the definition of UCBF​(h)\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h). If Pfail​(h)>P^fail​(h)P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)>\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h), then q=Pfail​(h)q=P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) lies in [P^fail​(h),1][\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h),1], and the KL event gives

kl(P^fail(h)∥Pfail(h))≤LFnF.\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\right)\leq\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}. (86)

Thus Pfail​(h)P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) is feasible in the supremum defining UCBF​(h)\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h), which implies

Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h).P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h). (87)

Combining the two cases gives

∀h∈ℋt:Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h).\forall h\in\mathcal{H}_{t}:P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h). (88)

Let ℰT\mathcal{E}_{T}, ℰF\mathcal{E}_{F}, and ℰR\mathcal{E}_{R} denote the target, falsification, and regression confidence events. Combining Eq. (75), Eq. (81), and Eq. (84), we have

ℙ⁡(ℰT∩ℰF∩ℰR)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{T}\cap\mathcal{E}_{F}\cap\mathcal{E}_{R}) =1−ℙ⁡(ℰTc∪ℰFc∪ℰRc)\displaystyle=1-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{T}^{c}\cup\mathcal{E}_{F}^{c}\cup\mathcal{E}_{R}^{c}) (89)
≥1−ℙ⁡(ℰTc)−ℙ⁡(ℰFc)−ℙ⁡(ℰRc)\displaystyle\geq 1-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{T}^{c})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{F}^{c})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{R}^{c})
≥1−αT−αF−αR\displaystyle\geq 1-\alpha_{T}-\alpha_{F}-\alpha_{R}
=1−α.\displaystyle=1-\alpha.

On this event, all three bounds in Eq. (69) hold simultaneously for every h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t}. This proves the lemma. ∎

B.5 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

By Lemma 3, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, all h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} simultaneously satisfy

G⁡(h)≥LCBT​(h),Pfail​(h)≤UCBF​(h),Dreg​(h)≤UCBR​(h).G(h)\geq\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h),\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h),\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h). (90)

This proves Eq. (11).

Now suppose that hh satisfies the confidence-gated commitment rule:

LCBT​(h)≥η,UCBF​(h)≤δ,UCBR​(h)≤β.\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h)\geq\eta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h)\leq\beta. (91)

For target-transfer gain, Eq. (90) and Eq. (91) imply

G⁡(h)\displaystyle G(h) ≥LCBT​(h)\displaystyle\geq\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h) (92)
≥η.\displaystyle\geq\eta.

For falsification risk,

Pfail​(h)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) ≤UCBF​(h)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h) (93)
≤δ.\displaystyle\leq\delta.

For regression damage,

Dreg​(h)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h) ≤UCBR​(h)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h) (94)
≤β.\displaystyle\leq\beta.

Combining Eq. (92), Eq. (93), and Eq. (94), we obtain

G⁡(h)≥η,Pfail​(h)≤δ,Dreg​(h)≤β.G(h)\geq\eta,\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta. (95)

This proves Eq. (13). ∎

B.6 Exact Probe Complexity Statement

We now give the exact finite-sample version of Corollary 1. Let ζT,ζR>0\zeta_{T},\zeta_{R}>0 be target and regression margins, and let 0≤δ−<δ≤10\leq\delta_{-}<\delta\leq 1 be empirical and population falsification thresholds.

Corollary 2 (Exact probe complexity).

Suppose

nT≥1+max⁡{8​LTζT2,28​LT3​ζT},n_{T}\geq 1+\max\left\{\frac{8L_{T}}{\zeta_{T}^{2}},\frac{28L_{T}}{3\zeta_{T}}\right\}, (96)
nR≥1+max⁡{2​LRζR2,14​LR3​ζR},n_{R}\geq 1+\max\left\{\frac{2L_{R}}{\zeta_{R}^{2}},\frac{14L_{R}}{3\zeta_{R}}\right\}, (97)

and

nF≥LFkl(δ−∥δ).n_{F}\geq\frac{L_{F}}{\mathrm{kl}(\delta_{-}\|\delta)}. (98)

Then, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, any h∈ℋth\in\mathcal{H}_{t} satisfying

G^​(h)≥η+ζT,P^fail​(h)≤δ−,D^reg​(h)≤β−ζR\widehat{G}(h)\geq\eta+\zeta_{T},\qquad\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta_{-},\qquad\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta-\zeta_{R} (99)

also satisfies

G⁡(h)≥η,Pfail​(h)≤δ,Dreg​(h)≤β.G(h)\geq\eta,\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta. (100)

Proof.

≤LR2​nR+7​LR3​(nR−1).\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{L_{R}}{2n_{R}}}+\frac{7L_{R}}{3(n_{R}-1)}.

nR≥2​LRζR2,n_{R}\geq\frac{2L_{R}}{\zeta_{R}^{2}}, (110)

then
