Combining Eq. (109), Eq. (111), and Eq. (113), we obtain

εR​(h)≤ζR.\varepsilon_{R}(h)\leq\zeta_{R}. (114)

We now control the falsification upper confidence bound. Assume P^fail​(h)≤δ−\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta_{-}. For fixed q=δq=\delta, the function p↦kl(p∥δ)p\mapsto\mathrm{kl}(p\|\delta) is decreasing on p∈[0,δ]p\in[0,\delta]. Indeed,

∂∂pkl(p∥δ)=logp⁡(1−δ)δ⁡(1−p),\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\mathrm{kl}(p\|\delta)=\log\frac{p(1-\delta)}{\delta(1-p)}, (115)

and for p<δp<\delta,

log⁡p⁡(1−δ)δ⁡(1−p)<0.\log\frac{p(1-\delta)}{\delta(1-p)}<0. (116)

Therefore,

kl(P^fail(h)∥δ)≥kl(δ−∥δ).\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|\delta\right)\geq\mathrm{kl}(\delta_{-}\|\delta). (117)

By Eq. (98),

LFnF≤kl(δ−∥δ)≤kl(P^fail(h)∥δ).\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}\leq\mathrm{kl}(\delta_{-}\|\delta)\leq\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|\delta\right). (118)

For fixed p=P^fail​(h)p=\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h), the map q↦kl(p∥q)q\mapsto\mathrm{kl}(p\|q) is increasing on q∈[p,1]q\in[p,1]. Hence every q>δq>\delta satisfies

kl(P^fail(h)∥q)>LFnF.\mathrm{kl}\left(\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\|q\right)>\frac{L_{F}}{n_{F}}. (119)

Thus no q>δq>\delta is feasible in the supremum defining UCBF​(h)\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h), and we have

UCBF​(h)≤δ.\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h)\leq\delta. (120)

Now suppose hh satisfies the empirical margin condition in Eq. (99). Combining Eq. (107), Eq. (114), and Eq. (120), we get

LCBT​(h)≥η,UCBF​(h)≤δ,UCBR​(h)≤β.\mathrm{LCB}_{T}(h)\geq\eta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{F}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad\mathrm{UCB}_{R}(h)\leq\beta. (121)

Applying Theorem 1 yields

G⁡(h)≥η,Pfail​(h)≤δ,Dreg​(h)≤β.G(h)\geq\eta,\qquad P_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)\leq\delta,\qquad D_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)\leq\beta. (122)

This proves the corollary. ∎

B.8 Remarks on Adaptivity and Scope Refinement

The proof requires that the final evaluation probes are not reused to construct or refine the hypothesis being certified. This condition prevents adaptive overfitting to the finite falsification set. In practice, this can be implemented in two equivalent ways. The first is sample splitting: use a development split for scope refinement and a fresh evaluation split for final commitment. The second is to define ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} as the enlarged finite set containing all hypotheses that can be produced by proposal and refinement before final evaluation; the same proof then applies with |ℋt||\mathcal{H}_{t}| replaced by the size of this enlarged set.

The theorem certifies reliability with respect to the probe-generation distributions 𝒟T​(h)\mathcal{D}_{T}(h), 𝒟F​(h)\mathcal{D}_{F}(h), and 𝒟R​(h)\mathcal{D}_{R}(h). If these distributions differ from the deployment distribution, an additional distribution-shift term is needed. For example, if the deployment falsification distribution is within total variation distance ρ\rho of 𝒟F​(h)\mathcal{D}_{F}(h), then the certified falsification risk increases by at most ρ\rho. The commitment gate controls statistical generalization from finite probes to the specified probe distributions, while the quality of the probe generator determines how well those distributions cover deployment-time boundary cases.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Details

C.1 Benchmark Details

Web and browser-control tasks.

For WebArena [Zhou et al., 2024] and BrowserGym [Le Sellier de Chezelles et al., 2025], we follow the official environment setup and success validators. Each task provides a natural-language instruction, an initial browser state, and an environment-specific completion condition. We use these validators as the verifier vhv_{h} whenever possible. For FGSE, target-transfer probes are constructed from tasks sharing the same high-level interaction pattern, while falsification probes are selected from tasks with similar surface forms but different completion conditions, websites, forms, or required constraints. Regression probes are drawn from previously solved held-out tasks and are never used to propose the candidate hypothesis.

Tool-use and app-interaction tasks.

For AppWorld [Trivedi et al., 2024], we evaluate on the official Normal and Challenge splits and report task-goal completion using the benchmark-provided database-state evaluator. For τ\tau-bench [Yao et al., 2024], we evaluate both retail and airline domains and use the official database-state comparison and passk\mathrm{pass}^{k} reliability protocol. In both benchmarks, a hypothesis may modify the agent’s tool-use policy, retrieval memory, or instruction-level strategy, but the available tools, API schemas, and domain policies are fixed across all methods. Holding tool access fixed isolates the effect of the update mechanism.

Security and adversarial tool-output tasks.

AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al., 2024] is used to evaluate whether self-evolution increases susceptibility to prompt injection or malicious tool outputs. We report utility success on benign tasks, security success under attacks, and the joint utility-security score. For FGSE, falsification probes include decoy tool outputs, conflicting instructions, and previously solved benign cases. A candidate update is rejected if it improves utility but increases attack success or violates a high-priority system or user constraint.

Long-term memory tasks.

For LongMemEval [Wu et al., 2024] and LoCoMo [Maharana et al., 2024], we evaluate whether committed hypotheses improve memory use without corrupting persistent user or task state. We report the official QA accuracy or F1 metrics, temporal reasoning accuracy, knowledge-update accuracy, and abstention accuracy when available. We also measure memory pollution rate, defined as the fraction of committed updates that are later contradicted by held-out evidence or cause a regression on archived successful examples.

Code and mathematical reasoning diagnostics.

We use HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021], MBPP [Austin et al., 2021], and SWE-bench Verified [Chowdhury et al., 2024] as verifier-rich coding environments because unit tests provide executable feedback. SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of the original SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2024], released by OpenAI in collaboration with the SWE-bench authors [Chowdhury et al., 2024]. We report pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP and resolved rate on SWE-bench Verified. For mathematical reasoning, we use GSM8K [Cobbe et al., 2021] and MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021], reporting exact-match solve rate after answer normalization. These datasets are used primarily for controlled analysis of update quality because their verifiers allow clean construction of target, boundary, and regression probes.

C.2 Evaluation Metrics

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote a held-out evaluation set and let v⁡(x,τ)∈[0,1]v(x,\tau)\in[0,1] be the benchmark-specific verifier score. The standard task success rate is

SR=1|𝒟|​∑x∈𝒟v⁡(x,τx).\mathrm{SR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}v(x,\tau_{x}). (123)

For binary task validators, this reduces to the fraction of solved tasks. For benchmarks with official non-binary scores, we use the official normalized score.

For each committed or rejected hypothesis hh, we compute the three FGSE-specific statistics:

G^​(h)=1|𝒯⁡(h)|​∑x∈𝒯⁡(h)[Jvh​(Θ⊕h,x)−Jvh​(Θ,x)],\widehat{G}(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{T}(h)}\left[J_{v_{h}}(\Theta\oplus h,x)-J_{v_{h}}(\Theta,x)\right], (124)
P^fail(h)=1|ℱ⁡(h)|∑x∈ℱ⁡(h)𝕀[Jvh(Θ⊕h,x)−Jvh(Θ,x)<−ϵ∨Eh(Θ⊕h,x)=0],\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{F}(h)}\mathbb{I}\left[J_{v_{h}}(\Theta\oplus h,x)-J_{v_{h}}(\Theta,x)<-\epsilon\;\vee\;E_{h}(\Theta\oplus h,x)=0\right], (125)
D^reg​(h)=1|ℛ⁡(h)|​∑x∈ℛ⁡(h)[Jvh​(Θ,x)−Jvh​(Θ⊕h,x)]+.\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}(h)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{R}(h)}\left[J_{v_{h}}(\Theta,x)-J_{v_{h}}(\Theta\oplus h,x)\right]_{+}. (126)

We also report:

  • •

    Harmful update rate: the fraction of committed updates that cause held-out regression larger than ϵ\epsilon.

  • •

    Accepted-update precision: the fraction of committed updates that yield positive held-out target-transfer gain without measurable regression.

  • •

    Falsification hit rate: the fraction of rejected or refined updates for which at least one falsification probe exposes a failure.

  • •

    Post-commit violation rate: the fraction of future activations where a committed hypothesis violates its expected-effect checker.

  • •

    Cost: total LLM calls, verifier calls, wall-clock time, and token usage per committed update.

C.3 Fair Comparison Protocol

All controlled comparisons follow the same protocol [Yang et al., 2026b]:

  1. 1.

    Same backbone: every method uses the same base LLM and the same ReAct-style executor unless the method intrinsically requires a different executor.

  2. 2.

    Same tools: all methods receive identical tool schemas, browser actions, API access, and environment observations.

  3. 3.

    Same memory budget: methods with persistent memory are allowed the same maximum number of stored units and the same retrieval top-kk.

  4. 4.

    Same update budget: methods that propose self-updates receive the same number of completed training episodes and the same maximum number of update attempts.

  5. 5.

    No test leakage: hypotheses, reflections, playbooks, workflows, and memory entries are constructed only from training or development episodes. Test tasks are used only for final evaluation.

  6. 6.

    Same verifier access: if a verifier is available during development, all methods may use it under the same budget. During final evaluation, verifier outputs are used only for scoring.

For workflow-search or architecture-search methods such as AFlow [Zhang et al., 2025a], ADAS [Hu et al., 2025], GPTSwarm [Zhuge et al., 2024], and MetaAgent [Zhang et al., 2025b], we report a controlled-budget version when code and prompts are available. Methods requiring a substantially larger search budget, extra training data, reinforcement learning, or model fine-tuning are reported in a separate native-setting table, outside the controlled FGSE comparisons.

C.4 Baseline Implementation Details

Direct and ReAct.

The direct baseline uses the base LLM without persistent memory or post-episode updates. The ReAct baseline [Yao et al., 2023] uses the same action space and tool interface as FGSE but does not modify its persistent state after each episode.

Self-Refine and Reflexion.

Self-Refine [Madaan et al., 2023] performs within-episode critique and revision under the same maximum number of refinement calls as FGSE’s hypothesis proposal calls. Reflexion [Shinn et al., 2023] writes natural-language reflections after failed or low-scoring episodes and retrieves them in future tasks. Reflexion commits reflections without requiring structured preconditions, falsification probes, or regression tests.

Voyager-style skill memory.

The Voyager-style baseline [Wang et al., 2023] stores reusable skills or lessons from successful episodes and retrieves them for related future tasks. For non-Minecraft benchmarks, we adapt the skill library into a text-based rule or tool-use strategy library while keeping the same retrieval budget as FGSE.

Memory and context-evolution methods.

A-Mem [Xu et al., 2025] is implemented as an agentic memory organization baseline that dynamically indexes, links, and updates memories. ACE [Zhang et al., 2026f] is implemented as an evolving playbook baseline that incrementally revises persistent context using execution feedback. Both methods are evaluated with the same memory capacity and retrieval top-kk as FGSE.

Workflow and agent-design optimization methods.

AFlow [Zhang et al., 2025a], ADAS [Hu et al., 2025], GPTSwarm [Zhuge et al., 2024], and MetaAgent [Zhang et al., 2025b] provide comparisons at the agentic-workflow level, complementing update-level memory methods. Because these methods may search over a larger design space than FGSE, we distinguish controlled-budget and native-budget results.

C.5 FGSE Hyperparameters

All hyperparameters are selected on development tasks and then fixed for test evaluation.

C.6 Ablation Studies

We conduct the following ablations:

  • •

    No falsification: commit every proposed hypothesis that improves the source episode.

  • •

    Random probes: replace targeted falsification probes with randomly sampled held-out tasks.

  • •

    LLM-judge gate: replace executable or environment verifiers with an LLM-only judgment.

  • •

    No regression archive: remove ℛ⁡(h)\mathcal{R}(h) from the commitment rule.

  • •

    No scope narrowing: reject all hypotheses that fail falsification without allowing precondition refinement.

  • •

    Free-form memory: store unstructured natural-language lessons instead of structured (ch,bh,eh,vh)(c_{h},b_{h},e_{h},v_{h}) hypotheses.

  • •

    Probe-budget sweep: vary the number of falsification probes to measure the trade-off between update safety and computation.

These ablations isolate whether FGSE’s gains come from verifier grounding, targeted counterexample construction, regression protection, structured update representation, or scope refinement.

C.7 Compute Resources

FGSE uses frozen language models without training or fine-tuning. All reported experiments access frozen LLM backbones through provider-hosted APIs, with no author-side GPU use for model training or inference. The provider-side serving compute for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and DeepSeek-V3.1 is not observable to us and is not included in the reported compute. Our local compute consists of agent orchestration, environment simulation, browser/app execution, sandboxed code execution, probe construction, verifier calls, logging, and result aggregation.

Unless otherwise stated, experiments were orchestrated on CPU workers with 8 vCPUs and 32GB memory per worker. For code-execution and repository-level diagnostics such as SWE-bench Verified, we used sandbox workers with 16 vCPUs and 64GB memory. We used up to 32 workers concurrently. We report compute in terms of LLM calls, verifier calls, parallel wall-clock time, and aggregate client-side CPU usage. One LLM call denotes one model completion request, including action generation, reflection, hypothesis proposal, scope refinement, and LLM-judge calls when used by a baseline. One verifier call denotes one execution of an official benchmark validator, unit test, database-state checker, security checker, or exact-match evaluator.

The full project also included preliminary diagnostics, pilot prompt variants, failed verifier configurations, and exploratory ablations that are not included in Table 4. These exploratory runs used approximately 1.6×1.6\times the compute of the final reported experiments. In total, the project used approximately 8.9×1058.9{\times}10^{5} LLM calls, 1.35×1061.35{\times}10^{6} verifier calls, and 7.9×1037.9{\times}10^{3} client CPU-hours. Most additional compute came from early probe-construction variants and unsuccessful target-only or LLM-judge gating configurations.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

D.1 Additional Reliability and Ablation Results

Memory and update reliability.

Table 5 further evaluates long-term memory performance and controlled self-evolution reliability. FGSE obtains the strongest memory performance while also reducing unsafe update commitment, falsification failure, and regression damage. These results support improving future target performance while preserving previously solved behaviors and rejecting overgeneralized updates.

Additional ablation results

Table6 presents the results of additional ablation experiments.

D.2 Update-Selection and Falsification Analysis

Plasticity–safety Pareto frontier

Effective self-evolution combines useful agent improvements with protection against harmful or regressive memory updates. We examine the plasticity–safety Pareto frontier for update selection and compare FGSE’s position with alternative strategies.

We sweep a broad range of update-selection configurations and compare representative strategies, including FGSE, FGSE w/o Refine, Target-Only, LLM-Judge Gate, Conservative Gate, Exhaustive Verifier, Random Keep, and No Persistent Update. For each configuration cc, we measure: (i) update gain Δupd​(c)\Delta_{\mathrm{upd}}(c), defined as the average improvement after applying the selected update; (ii) harmful update rate H⁡(c)H(c), i.e., the fraction of committed updates that later induce safety violations or incorrect behavior on held-out probes; (iii) regression damage R⁡(c)R(c), i.e., the average degradation on archived successful behaviors; and (iv) verifier cost C⁡(c)C(c), measured as the average number of verifier calls per candidate update. Figure 6 visualizes the resulting trade-off. The left panel plots Δupd\Delta_{\mathrm{upd}} against HH, while the right panel plots Δupd\Delta_{\mathrm{upd}} against RR. Each point corresponds to one configuration, point size encodes verifier cost, and the black dashed curve marks the empirical Pareto frontier.

Figure 6 reveals a clear plasticity–safety frontier. First, FGSE traces the dominant lower-right boundary in both panels over a broad range of medium-cost configurations, achieving substantially larger update gain at similar or lower harm than competing strategies. In the harmful-update panel, frontier configurations of FGSE achieve roughly 9%9\%–12%12\% update gain while keeping the harmful update rate within 2.5%2.5\%–4.5%4.5\%, typically with only 2020–4040 verifier calls per candidate update. At comparable gain levels, Target-Only and LLM-Judge Gate incur much larger harmful update rates, often exceeding 8%8\%–15%15\%, indicating that target improvement alone is an unreliable proxy for safe transfer.

Second, a purely conservative policy is also suboptimal. Conservative Gate combines low harm with much smaller update gain in the lower-left region. This shows that effective self-improvement also requires sufficient plasticity to capture reusable behavioral rules. Conversely, Exhaustive Verifier pushes harm slightly lower than FGSE in a few settings, but does so at much higher verifier cost and with little or no gain advantage, indicating that aggressive verification yields diminishing returns.

Third, the comparison between FGSE and FGSE w/o Refine highlights the functional role of scope refinement. Without refinement, many configurations move upward in both panels: they retain some gain but suffer higher harmful update rates and larger regression damage. This suggests that a substantial fraction of risky updates retain utility and become safe only after narrowing their applicability conditions. Overall, the Pareto analysis supports FGSE’s better trade-off between plasticity and safety, placing it in a more favorable region of the update-selection design space.

Targeted probes versus random probes.

FGSE uses targeted falsification: the verifier constructs probes likely to expose scope overreach, missing preconditions, archived regressions, and decoy-induced shortcut behavior. We compare targeted probe scheduling with budget-matched baselines to evaluate its efficiency in discovering harmful updates.

Let ℋbad\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}} denote the set of candidate updates that are in fact unsafe or regressive under held-out evaluation. Given a probe budget KK, we define the bad-update detection rate as

D(K)=1|ℋbad|∑h∈ℋbad[τh≤K],D(K)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}|}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\tau_{h}\leq K\right], (127)

where τh\tau_{h} is the number of probes required to expose update hh under a given scheduling policy. Thus, D⁡(K)D(K) measures the fraction of unsafe updates discovered within the first KK probes.

To account for the severity of detected updates, we also report harmful update avoided,

A⁡(K)=∑h∈ℋbadwh[τh≤K]∑h∈ℋbadwh,A(K)=\frac{\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}}w_{h}\,\mathbb{1}\!\left[\tau_{h}\leq K\right]}{\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bad}}}w_{h}}, (128)

where whw_{h} is the downstream harm weight of update hh, estimated from its induced violation severity and regression impact. Hence, A⁡(K)A(K) measures how much total harmful mass would be prevented if all detected bad updates were rejected before commitment.

We compare five probe-selection policies under the same verifier budget: Targeted (the full FGSE probe scheduler), Stratified Random (random selection balanced across probe sources), Pure Random (uniform sampling from the entire probe pool), Boundary-Only (target only applicability-boundary probes), and Regression-Only (target only archived-regression probes). Figure 7 plots the resulting falsification discovery curves.

Figure 7 shows that targeted probing is markedly more informative than random testing at every budget. The gap is largest in the practically relevant low-budget regime, where verifier calls are scarce. At around K=8K=8, the Targeted policy already detects roughly twice as many bad updates as Pure Random, and the improvement is even larger in terms of harmful update avoided. This indicates that targeted probing discovers more harmful updates early and prioritizes those with larger downstream damage.

A second observation is that Boundary-Only and Regression-Only each improve over pure random sampling in the regimes where their probe families are most relevant, but both eventually saturate below the full targeted strategy. This suggests that harmful updates are heterogeneous: some arise from overly broad applicability conditions, whereas others only become visible through archived-regression or decoy-style counterfactual tests. Therefore, a single probe family is insufficient; the gain of FGSE comes from selecting probes conditionally on the specific hypothesis under test.

Finally, the larger gap in A⁡(K)A(K) than in D⁡(K)D(K) is itself informative. It shows that targeted probing tends to surface the most dangerous updates first while increasing discovery count. This property is crucial for practical self-evolution, where only a small verifier budget is available and preventing a few highly harmful commitments is more important than marginally increasing average detection at very large budgets.

Stability under stochastic rollouts.

We evaluate each candidate hypothesis under multiple stochastic rollouts to assess the reproducibility of its benefit across seeds.

For a hypothesis hh and evaluation set 𝒳h\mathcal{X}_{h}, we define its seed-specific update effect as

Δh(s)=1|𝒳h|​∑x∈𝒳h(R⁡(π⊕h,x,s)−R⁡(π,x,s)),\Delta_{h}^{(s)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{h}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{h}}\Big(R(\pi\oplus h;x,s)-R(\pi;x,s)\Big), (129)

where ss is the rollout seed controlling stochastic decoding, action tie-breaking, and environment perturbations. Thus, Δh(s)\Delta_{h}^{(s)} measures the marginal effect of applying hypothesis hh under seed ss.

To quantify stability, we further compute the mean seed effect

Δ¯h=1S​∑s=1SΔh(s),\bar{\Delta}_{h}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\Delta_{h}^{(s)}, (130)

and the sign-consistency score

C(h)=1S∑s=1S[sign(Δh(s))=sign(Δ¯h)],C(h)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\Delta_{h}^{(s)}\big)=\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\bar{\Delta}_{h}\big)\right], (131)

which measures the fraction of seeds whose update effect agrees in sign with the mean effect. A stable and genuinely useful update should exhibit both a positive Δ¯h\bar{\Delta}_{h} and high sign consistency.

Figure 8 visualizes the seed-level effect distributions for representative hypotheses from the Commit, Refine, and Reject groups. Each row shows the distribution of Δh(s)\Delta_{h}^{(s)} over seeds for one hypothesis, using a raincloud plot. This visualization shows the robustness of observed gains across stochastic rollouts.

Figure 8 shows a clear separation between update classes. Committed hypotheses are tightly concentrated on the positive side, with small seed variance and high sign consistency. In our diagnostic run, the median committed hypothesis has Δ¯h≈0.10\bar{\Delta}_{h}\approx 0.10 and median sign consistency above 0.90.9, indicating that its positive effect persists across seeds. Refined hypotheses remain beneficial on average, but their distributions are wider and more sensitive to rollout randomness, which is consistent with the interpretation that they capture partially useful rules whose scope still requires tightening. In contrast, rejected hypotheses are typically centered near zero or slightly negative, and many of them flip sign across seeds, showing that their apparent gains are unstable and largely attributable to stochastic variation.

The effects of accepted updates persist across seeds. Hypothesis identity dominates rollout randomness as a source of variation. FGSE preferentially commits hypotheses whose benefit persists across stochastic executions.

Representative Commit–Refine–Reject Cases

We inspect three representative hypotheses from the development audit archive. Each case is evaluated under the default setting used in the main experiments: |T⁡(h)|=8|T(h)|=8, |F⁡(h)|=16|F(h)|=16, |R⁡(h)|=16|R(h)|=16, η=0.03\eta=0.03, δ=0.05\delta=0.05, and β=0.01\beta=0.01. We report the target-transfer gain G^​(h)\widehat{G}(h), falsification failure rate P^fail​(h)\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h), regression damage D^reg​(h)\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h), and the resulting gate decision. These cases illustrate how FGSE distinguishes transferable rules, repairable overgeneralizations, and unsafe shortcuts.

The default FGSE gate commits the round-trip booking rule and accepts the refined calendar rule after scope narrowing. In the refinement and rejection cases, falsification and regression evidence govern commitment alongside positive target-transfer gain. The refinement case demonstrates the practical value of one-pass scope narrowing: G^​(h)\widehat{G}(h) decreases moderately from 10.4%10.4\% to 7.6%7.6\%, but P^fail​(h)\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{fail}}(h) drops from 18.8%18.8\% to 0.0%0.0\%, and D^reg​(h)\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{reg}}(h) drops from 2.7%2.7\% to 0.8%0.8\%. Thus, under the default setting, FGSE preserves useful self-evolution while blocking the main failure modes exposed by falsification and regression probes.

D.3 Mechanistic Analysis of Long-Term Self-Evolution

Trajectory-level behavioral changes.

Aligned interpretability in autonomous driving ties language to intermediate perception, prediction, and planning outputs [Ding et al., 2025]. We compare baseline and FGSE execution trajectories to identify the dominant behavioral edits underlying performance improvements.

Let τB=(a1,…,aT)\tau^{\mathrm{B}}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{T}) and τF=(a1′,…,aT′′)\tau^{\mathrm{F}}=(a^{\prime}_{1},\dots,a^{\prime}_{T^{\prime}}) denote the baseline and FGSE trajectories for the same task. We first align the two traces at the action-type level and group all trajectory edits into four interpretable behavior families: tool order, memory retrieval, constraint checking, and final answer formatting. For each family e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, we compute its weighted edit mass

me​(τB,τF)=∑o∈𝒪ew⁡(o),m_{e}(\tau^{\mathrm{B}},\tau^{\mathrm{F}})=\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}_{e}}w(o), (132)

where 𝒪e\mathcal{O}_{e} is the set of aligned edit operations assigned to family ee, and w⁡(o)w(o) denotes the causal weight of operation oo estimated from its contribution to final task improvement. We then define the dominant edit family as

e⋆​(τB,τF)=arg⁡maxe∈ℰ​me​(τB,τF).e^{\star}(\tau^{\mathrm{B}},\tau^{\mathrm{F}})=\arg\max_{e\in\mathcal{E}}m_{e}(\tau^{\mathrm{B}},\tau^{\mathrm{F}}). (133)

To make the behavioral change interpretable, we further assign each trajectory pair a baseline behavior motif and an FGSE behavior motif, determined from the dominant failure pattern before the first decisive divergence and the dominant corrected pattern after refinement, respectively. Figure 9 aggregates all improved trajectory pairs into a three-stage Sankey diagram: baseline motif →\rightarrow dominant edit family →\rightarrow FGSE motif. The width of each band is proportional to the number of corrected trajectories contributing to that transition.

Figure 9 shows that FGSE’s gains are primarily driven by substantive behavioral correction. The dominant flow mass concentrates in three edit families: tool-order repair, constraint checking, and memory retrieval. Final-answer formatting occupies only a small portion of the total corrected mass and rarely converts failures to successes.

The largest transition typically starts from baseline traces with loose or misordered tool usage, passes through tool-order repair, and ends in ordered tool plans under FGSE. A similarly large portion of corrected trajectories flows through constraint checking, showing that many failures arise from missing explicit verification before tool execution or answer commitment despite available knowledge. Memory retrieval forms the third major band, and its contribution is especially prominent on long-horizon and memory-intensive tasks, where the baseline agent often fails to retrieve previously relevant context or latent facts.

Overall, the Sankey analysis clarifies where FGSE changes behavior: it reorganizes tool usage, retrieves missing evidence, and enforces explicit constraint checks. These findings strengthen the interpretation that FGSE improves the agent’s internal decision process.

D.4 Cost and Scalability

Memory-growth controllability.

We analyze memory-growth scalability by varying the retention budget and measuring how agent quality changes as the number of committed hypotheses increases. For each memory policy, we vary the nominal retention budget over

B∈{0,16,32,48,64,80,96,128,160,192,224,256,288,320},B\in\{0,16,32,48,64,80,96,128,160,192,224,256,288,320\},

and run long-horizon evaluation episodes under the same self-evolution protocol. For each run, we record the final committed memory size |ℳT||\mathcal{M}_{T}|, task success rate SR\mathrm{SR}, violation rate VR\mathrm{VR}, and average retrieval cost CretC_{\mathrm{ret}}. We compare All-Commit, FIFO Window, Similarity Top-kk, Value-Aware Pruning, and FGSE Selective Memory. Figure 10 presents the resulting memory-growth Pareto plot.

Figure 10 shows that memory growth is not monotonic in utility. The naive All-Commit strategy initially benefits from additional memory, but after the committed set becomes large, the curve enters an overgrown regime: success saturates and then degrades, while the violation rate rises steadily and retrieval cost increases sharply. In contrast, bounded heuristics such as FIFO Window and Similarity Top-kk keep memory smaller, but they also leave substantial performance on the table because they discard useful reusable rules too aggressively.

FGSE Selective Memory lies on the best empirical frontier in both panels. It reaches its strongest regime at a moderate memory size. In this diagnostic run, FGSE attains around 70%∼72%70\%\!\sim\!72\% task success once the committed memory reaches roughly 120120–150150 entries, while maintaining a violation rate near 4%∼5%4\%\!\sim\!5\%. At a comparable or even lower committed size, competing strategies either achieve lower success or incur substantially higher violation. Moreover, compared with All-Commit, FGSE achieves a clearly better quality–cost trade-off: it matches or exceeds the best success of naive growth using far fewer retained hypotheses and noticeably smaller retrieval cost. This indicates that memory quality and selective retention are the key bottleneck for gains from persistent memory.

Finally, the curves exhibit a visible saturation effect. Beyond a moderate memory size, the marginal gain of additional committed hypotheses becomes very small, while retrieval cost continues to increase. These results support controllable long-term memory growth through commitment filtered by utility, falsification, and regression preservation.

Appendix E Broader Impacts

FGSE may improve the reliability of long-horizon language agents by reducing unsafe memory updates, overgeneralized behavioral rules, and regressions on previously solved tasks. Potential positive impacts include safer agent adaptation in web, app, and tool-use settings where persistent memory is used. However, more reliable self-evolving agents may also increase the capability of automated systems that can perform harmful or unauthorized actions if deployed without access control, monitoring, and domain-specific safety constraints [Yang et al., 2026a, Fan et al., 2023]. Financial-agent audits likewise identify source-manipulation risks and motivate model-independent halts and hard loss limits [Wang and Saxena, 2026]. FGSE mitigates some of these risks through verifier-grounded falsification, regression testing, audit records, and post-commit monitoring. These mechanisms complement deployment-level safety controls.

Appendix F LLM Usage

This paper studies self-evolving LLM agents. In the experiments, frozen LLM backbones are used as ReAct-style executors that generate interaction trajectories in web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory environments. FGSE also uses an LLM-based proposer to convert episode evidence into structured candidate hypotheses. LLM-generated hypotheses enter verifier-based evaluation. The final commit–refine–reject decision is determined by target-transfer, falsification, and regression probes evaluated with executable or benchmark-provided verifiers, including official success validators, database-state checkers, unit tests, security validators, and exact-match evaluators.

During the broader research process, LLM-based tools assisted with wording, grammar, LaTeX formatting, code drafting, script debugging, and organization of experimental notes. The authors specified, checked, and approved all scientific claims, methodological choices, mathematical statements, proofs, experimental settings, reported numbers, figures, tables, and interpretations. They manually verified all references for existence, relevance, and correctness, and reviewed and edited LLM-assisted text and code before inclusion in the paper or experiments.
